full.text: Transpiration
The loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.
Water evaporates from the walls of mesophyll cells into air spaces and diffuses out through open stomata down a water potential gradient.
Factors that increase the rate
Importance
Transpiration pulls water up the xylem (the transpiration stream), carries mineral ions and cools the leaf.
The potometer measures water uptake, which is close to the rate of transpiration.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: A potometer measures water uptake, not transpiration directly. Some water is used in photosynthesis and to keep cells turgid.

items: Evaporation from mesophyll then diffusion out
Faster with heat, wind, light, low humidity
Creates the transpiration pull in xylem

full.text: Translocation in the phloem
The movement of organic solutes, mainly sucrose, through the phloem from sources to sinks.

items: Source: where sugars are made or released, such as mature leaves
Sink: where sugars are used or stored, such as roots, fruits and growing tips

full.text: Mass flow hypothesis

Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source with help from companion cells. This lowers the water potential, so water enters from the xylem by osmosis and the hydrostatic pressure rises. At the sink sucrose is removed, water leaves and the pressure falls. Sap flows from high to low pressure.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Ringing experiments and aphid stylets are classic evidence that sugars move in the phloem.

items: Sucrose moves in phloem, source to sink
Water enters by osmosis, pressure rises at source
Mass flow down the pressure gradient
Evidence: ringing, aphid stylets, radioactive tracers

full.text: Reproduction in flowering plants
Parts of a flower

items: Carpel: stigma, style and ovary containing ovules
Petals attract pollinators; sepals protect the bud

full.text: The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.
Pollination may be self-pollination or cross-pollination, by insects, wind, water or animals.
Double fertilisation
The pollen tube grows down the style and delivers two male nuclei. One fuses with the egg to form the zygote (2n); the other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm nucleus (3n).

written.stem: Describe four environmental factors that affect the rate of transpiration.
written.model_answer: Higher temperature increases evaporation and diffusion; lower humidity increases the water potential gradient; wind removes humid air near the leaf; light opens stomata, so all of these increase the rate.

written.stem: Explain the mass flow hypothesis of translocation.
written.model_answer: Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source, lowering water potential. Water enters from the xylem by osmosis, raising hydrostatic pressure. At the sink sucrose is unloaded and water leaves, lowering the pressure, so sap flows from source to sink.

points.text: Unloaded at sink; flows source to sink

written.stem: Describe double fertilisation in flowering plants.
written.model_answer: The pollen tube enters the ovule and releases two male nuclei. One fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote. The other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form a triploid endosperm nucleus.

points.text: Pollen tube delivers two male nuclei
Other fuses with polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm

written.stem: State the main function of each of the plant growth regulators auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin and ethylene.
written.model_answer: Auxin promotes cell elongation and phototropism; gibberellin promotes stem elongation and seed germination; cytokinin promotes cell division; ethylene promotes fruit ripening.

written.stem: Describe how water moves from the soil into the root and up to the leaves of a plant.
written.model_answer: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis because they have a lower water potential than the soil. It crosses the cortex by the apoplast and symplast pathways. At the endodermis the Casparian strip forces it into the symplast. It enters the xylem and is pulled up by transpiration pull, helped by cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls, and by root pressure.

written.stem: Explain how plants respond to light and gravity.
written.model_answer: Shoots show positive phototropism: auxin moves to the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards light. Shoots are negatively and roots positively gravitropic; in roots, auxin collects on the lower side and inhibits elongation, so the root bends downwards. These responses help leaves get light and roots get water and anchorage.

points.text: Auxin moves to shaded side, elongation

Auxin inhibits root elongation on lower side

ask.question: What is transpiration?
ask.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata. Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out down a water potential gradient. It pulls water up the xylem.

ask.question: How does translocation work?
ask.answer: Sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem sieve tubes at a source. Water follows by osmosis and raises the pressure. At the sink sucrose is removed and the pressure falls, so sap flows by mass flow from source to sink.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 4.6: Translocation in the phloem

ask.question: What is double fertilisation?
ask.answer: In flowering plants the pollen tube releases two male nuclei. One fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 4.9: Reproduction in flowering plants

ask.question: What is phototropism?
ask.answer: Phototropism is a growth response to the direction of light. In shoots, auxin moves to the shaded side and causes more cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 4.12: Plant responses to stimuli

ask.question: What does ethylene do in plants?
ask.answer: Ethylene is a gaseous plant growth regulator that promotes fruit ripening and the fall of leaves and fruits.
